subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Solve the Festival Budget
hook: Help Arjun and Priya plan a school festival by solving arithmetic expressions!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A practical 12-year-old helping organize a school event

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: The smart mathematician ensuring calculations are correct

slides.title: Arjun and Priya Solve the Festival Budget
Planning the School Festival
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya are asked to budget for the annual school festival. The principal says: Food costs 3,000, decorations cost 2,000, and prizes cost 1,500. What's the total? Priya writes: 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add costs to find the total budget.

image.alt: Planning the School Festival — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: What is an Arithmetic Expression?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to Arjun: An arithmetic expression is a mix of numbers and operations like +, −, ×, and ÷. We solve them step by step to get an answer.

points.label: Definition
points.text: An arithmetic expression is a combination of numbers and mathematical operations (+, −, ×, ÷) that we evaluate to get a single answer.

points.label: Example
points.text: 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 is an expression. Its answer is 6,500.

slides.inSimpleWords: An arithmetic expression is numbers and math symbols combined.

slides.title: Simple Addition Expression
slides.storyContext: Arjun quickly adds: 3,000 + 2,000 = 5,000. Then 5,000 + 1,500 = 6,500. Priya checks: Yes! The total festival budget is 6,500.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add numbers left to right.

slides.title: Order of Operations (BODMAS)
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Arjun: We follow BODMAS - Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. Always in that order! She writes: 2 + 3 x 4. Not 5 x 4 = 20. But 3 x 4 first = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

points.label: BODMAS Rule
points.text: Do Brackets first, then Orders (powers), then ÷ and ×, then + and −. Work left to right for equal priority.

points.label: Why Order Matters
points.text: Without BODMAS, the same expression could have different answers. BODMAS ensures everyone gets the same correct answer.

example.problem: Solve: 10 + 2 × 3

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply and divide before adding and subtracting.

image.alt: Order of Operations (BODMAS) — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: The Multiplication Trap
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: Wait, if I compute 2 + 3 × 4 by adding first, I get 5 × 4 = 20. But if I multiply first, I get 2 + 12 = 14. Which is right? Priya nods: That's why BODMAS exists. Multiply first. The answer is 14.

points.label: Common Mistake
points.text: Students often add first when they see 2 + 3 × 4, getting 20. But BODMAS says multiply first, giving 14.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always multiply or divide before adding or subtracting.

slides.title: Brackets Matter
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: What if I calculate (3 + 2) × 4? Priya nods. Brackets first! 3 + 2 = 5, then 5 × 4 = 20. Different from 3 + 2 × 4 = 3 + 8 = 11!

points.label: Brackets
points.text: Solve inside brackets first. (3 + 2) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20

points.label: Brackets Change Everything
points.text: Brackets force operations to happen in a different order than BODMAS normally says.

example.problem: Which is bigger: (2 + 3) × 5 or 2 + 3 × 5?

slides.inSimpleWords: Brackets are calculated first.

image.alt: Brackets Matter — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Challenge: Nested Brackets
slides.storyContext: Priya writes: What about ((5 + 3) × 2) ÷ 4? Arjun thinks step by step. First 5 + 3 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16, then 16 ÷ 4 = 4.

points.label: Nested Brackets
points.text: Solve the innermost brackets first, then work outward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work from innermost brackets outward.

slides.title: Solving the Budget Puzzle
slides.storyContext: A vendor offers: Buy 10 samosas at ₹5 each, or 20 at ₹4 each. Buy 2 of each offer! Priya writes: (10 × 5) + (20 × 4) = 50 + 80 = 130. Arjun checks her work. Perfect!

points.label: Real-world expressions
points.text: Food budgets need careful calculation with brackets and multiplication.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use math to plan real festivals and costs.

image.alt: Solving the Budget Puzzle — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Division and Multiplication Together
slides.storyContext: The budget has 12,000. It's split equally among 4 committees. Each gets 3,000. Then, each committee spends 2,000. How much is left total? Priya writes: (12,000 ÷ 4) - 2,000 = 3,000 - 2,000 = 1,000 per committee. Total left: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000.

example.solution: 24 ÷ 3 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16 (left to right for equal priority)

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide and multiply in the order they appear.

image.alt: Division and Multiplication Together — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Left-to-Right Rule for Equal Operations
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: When you have only + and −, or only × and ÷, work left to right. For example: 20 - 5 - 3. Start with 20 - 5 = 15, then 15 - 3 = 12.

points.label: Equal Priority
points.text: Operations of the same priority level (like + and −, or × and ÷) are solved left to right.

slides.inSimpleWords: When operations have equal priority, go left to right.

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Operations
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries a tough one: 5 + 6 × 2 - 4 ÷ 2. Priya guides: Multiply and divide first. 6 × 2 = 12. 4 ÷ 2 = 2. Now: 5 + 12 - 2 = 17 - 2 = 15.
slides.inSimpleWords: Apply BODMAS: do × and ÷ first, then + and −.

slides.title: The Final Calculation
slides.storyContext: Principal asks: If we spend 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 today and get a 10% discount on food, what's the final cost? Priya calculates: 10% of 3,000 = 300. So (3,000 - 300) + 2,000 + 1,500 = 2,700 + 2,000 + 1,500 = 6,200.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use expressions to calculate real budgets with discounts.

image.alt: The Final Calculation — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Percent and Expressions
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: Percentages are part of expressions too. 10% means 1/10. So 10% of 3,000 = (10/100) × 3,000 = 0.1 × 3,000 = 300. Then subtract from the original.

points.label: Percent Calculation
points.text: Percent of a number = (percent/100) × number

example.problem: Find 20% of 5,000

slides.inSimpleWords: Percent = (number/100) × value.

slides.title: Budget with Tax
slides.storyContext: A new scenario: The decorations cost 2,000, and tax is 5%. What's the final cost? Priya: Tax = 5% of 2,000 = 0.05 × 2,000 = 100. Final = 2,000 + 100 = 2,100.

points.label: Adding Tax
points.text: Final price = original price + (tax% of original price)

example.problem: Cost ₹1,000 with 8% tax. Final cost?

slides.inSimpleWords: Tax is added to the original price.

slides.title: Challenge: Budget with Discount and Tax
slides.storyContext: Arjun faces a complex problem: Food costs 3,000. There's a 10% discount and then 5% tax on the discounted price. Priya works it: Discount = 0.1 × 3,000 = 300. Price after discount = 3,000 - 300 = 2,700. Tax = 0.05 × 2,700 = 135. Final = 2,700 + 135 = 2,835.

points.label: Two-step calculation
points.text: First apply discount, then calculate tax on the reduced price.

example.problem: ₹5,000 with 20% discount, then 8% tax on discounted price

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply discount first, then tax on the new price.

slides.title: Simplifying Expressions
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun: Sometimes expressions look long but they simplify. For instance: 100 + 50 + 25 + 25 can be grouped as (100 + 50) + (25 + 25) = 150 + 50 = 200.

points.label: Grouping
points.text: You can group numbers with + in any way — the answer stays the same. This is the associative property.

slides.inSimpleWords: Group numbers to make addition easier.

slides.title: Checking Work with Reverse Operations
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: How do I know my answer is right? Priya says: Use reverse operations! If you add, subtract back to check. She calculates 6,200 - 1,500 = 4,700, then 4,700 - 2,000 = 2,700. Yes, it all adds up to 6,200!

points.label: Verification
points.text: Reverse the operations to check: 6,200 - 1,500 - 2,000 = 2,700 (the remaining cost)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use reverse operations to verify your answers.

slides.title: Checking by Estimation
slides.storyContext: Another way to check: round numbers and estimate. 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 is roughly 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 ≈ 6,000 to 7,000. Our exact answer of 6,500 fits in that range!

points.label: Estimation Check
points.text: Round each number and estimate the sum. Compare with the exact answer to verify it makes sense.

example.solution: Rough: 4,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = 9,000. Yes, 9,200 is close and reasonable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Estimate to check if your exact answer is reasonable.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Step Festival Budget
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya tackle the real problem: Food ₹3,000 (10% discount). Decorations ₹2,000. Prizes ₹1,500 (5% tax). Calculate total. Food = 3,000 - 300 = 2,700. Decorations = 2,000. Prizes = 1,500 + 75 = 1,575. Total = 2,700 + 2,000 + 1,575 = 6,275.

points.label: Real-world complexity
points.text: Different items have different discounts or taxes. Calculate each, then add.

example.problem: Item A: ₹1,000 with 10% discount. Item B: ₹500. Item C: ₹800 with 5% tax. Total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Handle each item's discount or tax separately, then sum.

slides.title: Documenting the Success
slides.storyContext: The team documents everything in a notebook. Each calculation, each step, each total. By writing it down clearly, they can review it anytime and spot errors quickly.

points.label: Importance of Writing
points.text: Writing down all steps makes it easy to check work and find mistakes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Write out your work to catch errors.

slides.title: Powers in Arithmetic Expressions
slides.storyContext: Priya introduces a new topic: Sometimes expressions have powers, like 2^3 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Powers are solved after brackets but before multiplication. So 2 + 3^2 = 2 + 9 = 11.

points.label: Orders (Powers)
points.text: Powers like 2^3 are solved after brackets, before multiplication. Example: 3^2 = 9

example.problem: Solve: 5 + 2^3

slides.inSimpleWords: Powers are solved early in BODMAS, after brackets.

slides.title: Challenge: Expressions with Powers
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves: (2 + 1)^2 × 3 - 5. Priya guides: Brackets first: (2 + 1) = 3. Then power: 3^2 = 9. Then multiply: 9 × 3 = 27. Finally subtract: 27 - 5 = 22.

points.label: Full BODMAS with Powers
points.text: Remember: Brackets, Orders (powers), Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Powers follow brackets in BODMAS priority.

slides.title: Summary: BODMAS Hierarchy
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a poster: Remember the order. (1) Brackets, (2) Orders (powers), (3) Division and Multiplication (left to right), (4) Addition and Subtraction (left to right).

points.label: The Full Hierarchy
points.text:
1. Brackets
2. Orders (exponentials)
3. Division and Multiplication (left to right)
4. Addition and Subtraction (left to right)

slides.inSimpleWords: BODMAS tells you what to do first in any expression.

slides.title: Challenge: Audit Real Festival Budgets
slides.storyContext: Priya gives three festival budgets with mixed operations, discounts, and taxes. Arjun applies BODMAS to each and finds total costs. This real-world practice cements his understanding.

points.label: Mastery Through Practice
points.text: Apply BODMAS to complex, multi-item budget scenarios with varied operations.

example.problem: Budget: (1500 + 2500) × 0.9 + 500. Final total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve complex real budgets using BODMAS.

slides.title: Arjun and Priya's Success
slides.storyContext: The festival is a hit! Arjun and Priya present the final report: Total spent = 6,200. Budget left = 800. The principal smiles. You solved this with perfect arithmetic!

points.label: Arithmetic Mastery
points.text: Use BODMAS, brackets, and careful order to solve real problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arithmetic expressions solve real-world budgets and plans.

image.alt: Arjun and Priya's Success — Arithmetic Expressions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Explore Geometry
hook: Discover points, lines, and angles in the world around you with Arjun and Priya!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious builder who sees shapes in buildings

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A geometry expert explaining the world's structure

slides.title: A Tiny Dot and Endless Lines
slides.storyContext: Walking through Delhi, Arjun spots a dusty ground. He draws a single dot with his finger. What's that? he asks. Priya replies: That's a point - it has no length, width, or height. It's just a location! Then she draws a line through it. A line goes on forever in both directions!
slides.inSimpleWords: A point is a tiny location. A line goes forever.

image.alt: A Tiny Dot and Endless Lines — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Points: The Foundation of Geometry
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: A point is the most basic object in geometry. It has position but no size. We name it with capital letters, like point A or point P.

points.label: What is a Point?
points.text: A point has no length, width, or height. It only has a location. It is represented by a dot and named with a capital letter.

points.label: In Real Life
points.text: A pushpin in a map, a star in the night sky, a corner of a room — all are like points.

slides.inSimpleWords: A point is just a position with no size.

slides.title: Lines: Infinite and Straight
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a line on paper and extends it with arrows on both ends. This line has no beginning and no end. It goes on forever. A line passes through infinite points.

points.label: What is a Line?
points.text: A line is straight and goes on infinitely in both directions. It is made up of infinite points. It has no thickness.

points.label: Naming Lines
points.text: A line passing through points A and B is called line AB or line BA. Symbol: line AB (written with a line over AB)

slides.inSimpleWords: A line is straight and goes forever in both ways.

slides.title: Understanding Points and Lines
slides.storyContext: Arjun points at the horizon. The horizon looks like a line! Priya nods. Yes, though it's not truly infinite. But in geometry, we imagine lines that truly go forever.

points.label: Examples in Nature
points.text: The horizon, power lines, train tracks — they look like lines but are finite. True geometric lines are infinite.

example.problem: How many points lie on a line?
example.solution: Infinite points lie on any line. You can always find points between any two points on a line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines contain infinitely many points.

slides.title: Line Segments and Rays
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: A line segment is part of a line - it has two endpoints. Like the edge of a door. She draws a segment. A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. Like a laser beam!

points.label: Segments vs. Rays
points.text: Line segment: two endpoints (finite). Ray: one endpoint, goes forever in one direction.

points.label: Naming
points.text: Segment AB has endpoints A and B. Ray AB starts at A and goes through B forever.

example.problem: Name the line segment between points A and B.

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends. A ray has one end.

image.alt: Line Segments and Rays — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Where Lines Meet — Angles
slides.storyContext: They look at a street corner where two roads meet. That's an angle! says Priya, pointing. Two rays meeting at a point, called the vertex. The space between them is the angle. She shows Arjun with her arms. 90 degrees is a right angle - like a corner of a book!

points.label: Angle Basics
points.text: Two rays from one point form an angle. The point is the vertex. Angles measured in degrees. 90° = right angle.

example.problem: What's the angle at the corner of a square book?

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure the space between two rays.

image.alt: Where Lines Meet — Angles — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Types of Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun three angles on a poster. An acute angle is sharp (less than 90°). A right angle is exactly 90° (like a corner). An obtuse angle is wide (between 90° and 180°).

points.label: Acute Angle
points.text: Less than 90°. Example: 45°, 60°, 75°.

points.label: Right Angle
points.text: Exactly 90°. Found at corners of squares and rectangles.

points.label: Obtuse Angle
points.text: Between 90° and 180°. Example: 120°, 135°, 150°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles can be sharp, right, or wide.

slides.title: Challenge: Measure Angles Around You
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks around the classroom. The corner of his desk is a right angle (90°). The angle between the wall and the door is also 90°. The angle of the roof is acute (maybe 60°).

points.label: Estimation
points.text: You can estimate angles by comparing them to known angles like 90° or 45°.

example.problem: Is the angle of a ladder leaning against a wall acute, right, or obtuse?

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify angles in everyday objects.

slides.title: Parallel Lines Never Meet
slides.storyContext: Walking past railway tracks, Arjun points: Look - two lines that never meet! Priya nods: These are parallel lines. They stay the same distance apart forever. Watch how the electricity wires above do the same thing!

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Lines that never meet, no matter how far they extend. Stay the same distance apart.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines never cross or touch.

image.alt: Parallel Lines Never Meet — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Defining Parallel Lines
slides.storyContext: Priya formalizes: Two lines in the same plane are parallel if they never intersect. They stay equidistant (same distance) apart. Symbol: ∥ (written as line AB ∥ line CD).

points.label: Mathematical Definition
points.text: Parallel lines are lines in the same plane that never meet and maintain constant distance.

points.label: Key Property
points.text: If you measure the perpendicular distance from any point on one line to the parallel line, the distance is always the same.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines are equidistant and never meet.

slides.title: Intersecting Lines and Angles
slides.storyContext: Two roads cross in an X shape. When lines intersect, Priya explains, they create 4 angles. Opposite angles are equal! She measures with a protractor. This angle is 60 degrees. The opposite is also 60 degrees!

points.label: Vertical Angles
points.text: When two lines cross, opposite angles are equal.

example.problem: If one angle is 70°, what's the opposite angle?

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at intersections are always equal.

image.alt: Intersecting Lines and Angles — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Adjacent Angles and Linear Pairs
slides.storyContext: When two lines intersect, adjacent angles (next to each other) sum to 180°. This is called a linear pair. If one angle is 60°, the adjacent angle is 180° - 60° = 120°.

points.label: Linear Pair
points.text: Two adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

points.label: Property
points.text: If angle A = 60°, then its adjacent angle = 180° - 60° = 120°.

example.problem: One angle is 45°. What's its adjacent angle on a straight line?

slides.inSimpleWords: Adjacent angles on a line always sum to 180°.

slides.title: Challenge: Angle Relationships
slides.storyContext: Arjun is given two intersecting lines with one angle marked as 55°. Can he find all other angles? He reasons: Opposite angle = 55°. Adjacent angles = 180° - 55° = 125° each.

points.label: Finding All Angles
points.text: From one angle, you can find all others using: vertical angles are equal, and linear pairs sum to 180°.

example.problem: Two lines intersect with angle A = 80°. Find angles B, C, D.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use angle relationships to find all angles.

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun three angles: a sharp one (acute), a square corner (right), and a wide one (obtuse). An acute angle is less than 90°. A right angle is exactly 90°. An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. Arjun laughs. Like faces - happy (acute), neutral (right), surprised (obtuse)!

points.label: Angle Types
points.text: Acute: < 90°. Right: = 90°. Obtuse: > 90° but < 180°. Straight: = 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are sharp, square, or wide.

image.alt: Acute, Right, and Obtuse — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Straight Angle and Reflex Angle
slides.storyContext: Priya continues the angle types: A straight angle is exactly 180° — like a straight line. A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°. An angle of 270° is a reflex angle.

points.label: Straight Angle
points.text: An angle of 180°. It looks like a straight line.

points.label: Reflex Angle
points.text: An angle between 180° and 360°. It's the 'outside' angle when you measure the long way around.

example.problem: A clock hand moves 270°. Is that a reflex angle?
example.solution: Yes, 270° is greater than 180°, so it's a reflex angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Straight angles are 180°. Reflex angles are bigger.

slides.title: Measuring Angles with a Protractor
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to use a protractor. He places it at the vertex of an angle and aligns one ray with the 0° mark. The other ray shows the angle measure. For example, if one ray aligns with 50°, that's an acute angle of 50°.

points.label: Using a Protractor
points.text: 1. Place the center on the vertex. 2. Align one ray with 0°. 3. Read where the other ray crosses the scale.

example.problem: Measure an angle using a protractor.
example.solution: Place center on vertex, align baseline, read the scale where the angle ends.

slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor helps you measure angles precisely.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Angle Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arjun a tricky problem: Three rays start from point A. Ray AB makes 40° with ray AC. Ray AD makes 70° with ray AC. What angle does ray AB make with ray AD? Arjun figures: If both are measured from AC, and they're on opposite sides, then 40° + 70° = 110°.

points.label: Multiple Rays
points.text: When multiple rays start from a point, angles between them can be added or subtracted based on their relative positions.

example.problem: Ray 1 is 30° from Ray 2. Ray 2 is 50° from Ray 3. What's the angle from Ray 1 to Ray 3?
example.solution: If they're on the same side: 30° + 50° = 80°. If opposite sides: |50° - 30°| = 20°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add or subtract angles based on their arrangement.

slides.title: Geometry in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Priya points out buildings in Delhi. See the angles of the roof? The parallel lines of the windows? The perpendicular edges? Geometry is not just theory. It's the blueprint of the world.

points.label: Practical Geometry
points.text: Architects use points, lines, and angles to design beautiful and stable structures.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real buildings are built with geometry.

slides.title: Collinear and Non-Collinear Points
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws three points on a line. Priya says: These three points are collinear — they all lie on the same line. Now she draws three points not on the same line. These are non-collinear points.

points.label: Collinear Points
points.text: Points that lie on the same line.

points.label: Non-Collinear Points
points.text: Points that do not lie on the same line.

example.problem: Are points A(1,1), B(2,2), C(3,3) collinear?
example.solution: Yes, they lie on the same straight line y = x

slides.inSimpleWords: Collinear points are on the same line.

slides.title: Distance Between Points
slides.storyContext: Priya introduces the concept: The distance between two points is how far apart they are. If they're at the same location, the distance is 0. The farther apart they are, the greater the distance.

points.label: Measuring Distance
points.text: Distance between two points is the length of the line segment connecting them.

example.problem: Point A is at 0 cm, Point B is at 5 cm on a ruler. What's the distance?

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is how far apart two points are.

slides.title: Marking Points on a Line
slides.storyContext: Arjun marks several points on a line with equal spacing. Priya nods: These points divide the line into equal segments. They're equally spaced.

points.label: Equal Spacing
points.text: Points can be placed at regular intervals on a line to create equal segments.

slides.inSimpleWords: Points can divide lines into equal parts.

slides.title: Challenge: Geometry in Maps
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya mark key landmarks on their city map. They identify which pairs of landmarks connect with parallel streets, which with intersecting streets, and which are perpendicular to major roads.

points.label: Real-World Mapping
points.text: Maps show real geometry of cities using points (landmarks), lines (streets), and angles (intersections).

example.problem: A city has 3 parallel roads. How many intersections can a perpendicular road make?
example.solution: 3 intersections — one with each parallel road

slides.inSimpleWords: Maps use points, lines, and angles.

slides.title: The Geometry All Around
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Arjun and Priya look at the city skyline - dots of lights, lines of streets, angles of buildings. Geometry is everywhere! says Arjun. Priya smiles. Yes. Points, lines, and angles build our world.

points.label: Geometry Fundamentals
points.text: Points, lines, segments, rays, angles, and their relationships form the foundation of all shapes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry is the study of space, points, and shapes.

image.alt: The Geometry All Around — A Peek Beyond the Point

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Navigate City Streets
hook: Discover how parallel and intersecting lines shape our cities!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious navigator mapping city patterns

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A geometry expert explaining street designs

slides.title: Arjun and Priya Navigate City Streets
A Grid of Streets
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya look at a city map. Notice the pattern? says Priya. North-South streets run parallel - they never meet. East-West streets also run parallel. But North-South and East-West streets intersect at right angles! Arjun traces with his finger. Like a giant grid!
slides.inSimpleWords: Cities are laid out with parallel and intersecting streets.

image.alt: A Grid of Streets — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Parallel Lines — Always the Same Distance
slides.storyContext: They measure two North-South streets. These are always 500 meters apart, Priya explains, pointing at her map. No matter how far north or south you go, they stay 500 meters apart. That makes them parallel.

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Lines that never intersect and maintain constant distance apart. Symbol: ∥

example.problem: Are railway tracks parallel?
example.solution: Yes, they maintain equal distance and never meet

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines stay the same distance forever.

image.alt: Parallel Lines — Always the Same Distance — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Why Parallel Lines Are Important
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Why are parallel streets useful? Priya explains: Because they're predictable. You know they'll never crash into each other. City planners love parallel lines — they make neat grids and easy navigation.

points.label: Real-World Use
points.text: Parallel lines ensure predictable patterns. Cities, checkerboards, railroad tracks, and building designs all use parallels.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines make organized, predictable patterns.

slides.title: Intersecting Lines and Their Angles
slides.storyContext: At a road crossing, Priya sets up a protractor. When two lines intersect, they create four angles. Watch! She points. The angle on the top-left and bottom-right are equal. The angle on the top-right and bottom-left are also equal! Arjun checks: 65° and 65°! And 115° and 115°!

points.label: Vertical Angles
points.text: When two lines intersect, opposite angles are equal.

example.problem: Two lines intersect. One angle is 45°. Find the other three angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at intersections are always equal.

image.alt: Intersecting Lines and Their Angles — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: All Angles at an Intersection Sum to 360°
slides.storyContext: Priya points out: If you add all four angles at an intersection, you get 360°. For instance: 65° + 115° + 65° + 115° = 360°. That's a full rotation!

points.label: Total Angle
points.text: All angles around a point sum to 360°.

example.problem: Four angles at an intersection: 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°. Sum?

slides.inSimpleWords: All angles around a point = 360°.

slides.title: A Transversal Cuts Through Parallel Lines
slides.storyContext: Priya draws three lines on paper: two parallel horizontal lines, and one diagonal line cutting through both. This diagonal is a transversal - it intersects both parallel lines! Arjun asks: Do the angles match? Priya smiles. Yes! Corresponding angles are equal!

points.label: Transversal Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines: corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: A transversal cuts parallel lines at matching angles.

image.alt: A Transversal Cuts Through Parallel Lines — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Corresponding Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles in the same position at each intersection are equal. These are corresponding angles. If angle 1 is 60°, then angle 5 (in the same position at the lower intersection) is also 60°.

points.label: Corresponding Angles
points.text: When a transversal cuts parallel lines, angles in matching positions are equal.

points.label: Visual
points.text: Imagine the transversal creating 4 angles at the top intersection and 4 at the bottom. Angles 1 and 5, 2 and 6, 3 and 7, 4 and 8 are corresponding.

example.problem: A transversal crosses parallel lines. One angle is 55°. What's the corresponding angle at the other intersection?

slides.inSimpleWords: Matching angles at parallel-line intersections are equal.

slides.title: Alternate Interior Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya draws more lines. Between the two parallel lines, there are four angles. The angles on opposite sides of the transversal are called alternate interior angles. They're equal too! If one is 70°, its alternate interior angle is also 70°.

points.label: Alternate Interior Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, angles on opposite sides of the transversal (and between the parallel lines) are equal.

example.problem: A transversal crosses parallel lines. Alternate interior angle A = 80°. What's the other alternate interior angle?

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles on opposite sides of the transversal are equal.

slides.title: Finding Angles with a Transversal
slides.storyContext: A slanted power line (transversal) crosses two parallel streets. Priya measures one angle: 70°. By the transversal property, the corresponding angle at the other street is also 70°. And the alternate angle is 70° too! Arjun nods. Geometry is predictable!

points.label: Angle Relationships
points.text: Corresponding angles are equal. Alternate interior angles are equal. Co-interior angles sum to 180°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines at 60°. What's the alternate interior angle?

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles match when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.

image.alt: Finding Angles with a Transversal — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Co-Interior Angles (Consecutive Interior Angles)
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: On the same side of the transversal, between the parallel lines, are co-interior angles. These don't equal each other — they sum to 180°! If one is 60°, the other is 120°.

points.label: Co-Interior Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, co-interior angles (on the same side, between the parallels) sum to 180°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses parallel lines. One co-interior angle is 75°. What's the other?

slides.inSimpleWords: Same-side interior angles sum to 180°.

slides.title: Challenge: Angle Relationships with Parallel Lines
slides.storyContext: Arjun is given two parallel lines and a transversal. One angle is 45°. Can he find all 8 angles formed? He reasons: Corresponding angles = 45° (there are 4 of them). Alternate interior = 45°. Co-interior = 180° - 45° = 135°.

points.label: Finding All Angles
points.text: From one angle at a transversal-parallel intersection, you can find all 8 angles using angle relationships.

example.problem: Given one angle is 50°, find all 8 angles at the two intersections.
example.solution: Angles: 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (at first intersection); 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (at second) due to corresponding angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use relationships to find all angles.

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines — The 90-Degree Special
slides.storyContext: They spot a lamp post standing straight up, crossing a horizontal cable. These lines are perpendicular, says Priya. They intersect at exactly 90 degrees. Arjun checks with a square corner. Perfect! Symbol is ⊥.

points.label: Perpendicular Lines
points.text: Lines that intersect at 90 degrees. Symbol: ⊥

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular lines cross at right angles (90°).

image.alt: Perpendicular Lines — The 90-Degree Special — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Perpendicular lines are everywhere: corners of buildings, edges of paper, crossroads with right-angle turns, the axes of a coordinate plane. They're fundamental to construction and design.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if they intersect at a 90° angle.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Written as line AB ⊥ line CD

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular lines are everywhere in buildings and design.

slides.title: Drawing Perpendicular Lines
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to draw perpendiculars using a set square. He places the set square with its right angle corner on the line, then marks a perpendicular line. Priya checks with a protractor: exactly 90°!

points.label: Method 1: Set Square
points.text: Place the right angle of a set square on the line and mark the perpendicular direction.

points.label: Method 2: Protractor
points.text: Use a protractor to measure 90° from the original line.

example.problem: Draw a line perpendicular to line AB at point P on AB.
example.solution: Use a set square or compass to construct a 90° angle at P.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use tools to draw 90° angles.

slides.title: Challenge: Perpendicular and Parallel Combined
slides.storyContext: Priya gives a complex problem: Two parallel lines with a perpendicular transversal. What are all the angles? Arjun reasons: Perpendicular transversal means all angles = 90°!

points.label: Special Case
points.text: When a transversal is perpendicular to parallel lines, all 8 angles are 90°.

example.problem: A transversal is perpendicular to two parallel lines. What are all 8 angles?

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular transversals create all right angles.

slides.title: Mapping the City Grid
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya mark a small section of Delhi on their map. They identify which streets are parallel, which intersect, and which are perpendicular. The pattern emerges: organized, logical, and mathematical.

points.label: Urban Design
points.text: Cities are designed using parallel and perpendicular lines to create efficient, navigable grids.

slides.inSimpleWords: City grids use parallel and perpendicular lines.

slides.title: Exterior Angles on the Same Side
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, angles outside (exterior to) the parallel lines on the same side are called co-exterior angles. They sum to 180°, just like co-interior angles.

points.label: Co-Exterior Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, co-exterior angles (on the same side, outside the parallels) sum to 180°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses parallel lines. One co-exterior angle is 100°. What's the other?

slides.inSimpleWords: Exterior angles on the same side sum to 180°.

slides.title: Alternate Exterior Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya draws: Angles outside the parallel lines but on opposite sides of the transversal are alternate exterior angles. Like alternate interior angles, they're equal! If one is 60°, the other is also 60°.

points.label: Alternate Exterior Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, angles outside (and on opposite sides) are equal.

example.problem: A transversal crosses parallel lines. One exterior angle is 75°. What's the alternate exterior angle?

slides.inSimpleWords: Exterior angles on opposite sides are equal.

slides.title: Challenge: All 8 Angles — Full Mastery
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arjun the ultimate test: Two parallel lines, a transversal at 35°. Find all 8 angles. Arjun identifies: 35° (one pair of corresponding angles), 145° (supplementary to 35°), plus their opposites and alternates. He finds: 35°, 145°, 35°, 145° (at each intersection), plus their alternate counterparts.

points.label: Comprehensive Angle Analysis
points.text: From one angle, identify all 8 angles using: vertical angles, corresponding angles, alternate angles, and supplementary angles.

example.problem: One angle is 42° where a transversal crosses parallel lines. Find all angles.
example.solution: 42° appears 4 times (corresponding and alternate). 138° appears 4 times (supplementary).

slides.inSimpleWords: Master all 8 angles from one given angle.

slides.title: Intersecting at Different Angles
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: What if a transversal crosses parallel lines at an angle that's NOT 90 degrees? Priya draws one at 45 degrees. Then 60 degrees. Each creates different angle measures, but the relationships stay the same: corresponding = corresponding, alternate = alternate, co-interior = 180.

points.label: Angle Relationships Hold
points.text: The relationship between angles is independent of the specific angle measure. The rules always apply.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angle relationships work for any angle measure.

slides.title: Three Parallel Lines and Two Transversals
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya add a third parallel line and a second transversal to their diagram. Now there are even more angles! Priya: But the same rules apply. Track which angles correspond, which are alternate, which are supplementary.

points.label: Complex Configurations
points.text: Even with multiple parallel lines and transversals, angle relationships remain consistent.

example.problem: Three parallel lines, two transversals. How many angle intersections are there?

slides.inSimpleWords: Angle rules scale to more complex configurations.

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Perfect City Grid
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya design a small grid section: 3 parallel North-South streets and 3 parallel East-West streets, all perpendicular to each other. They mark all intersections, measure all angles (all 90°), and verify every relationship.

points.label: Grid Construction
points.text: A perfect city grid uses parallel lines that are perpendicular to another set of parallel lines, creating all right angles.

example.problem: A 3×3 city grid of perpendicular streets. How many intersections?

slides.inSimpleWords: Design grids with parallel and perpendicular lines.

slides.title: City Geometry Unlocked
slides.storyContext: Walking home through the planned city streets, Arjun points out parallel lines, intersections, and perpendicular lamp posts. Our city is built on geometry! he says. Priya agrees. And now you can read it all!

points.label: Summary
points.text: Parallel lines stay apart. Intersecting lines cross. Transversals create angle relationships. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel and intersecting lines design cities.
